test_title: RRB ALP CBT-II (Electrician) Official Paper (Held On: 02 May, 2025 Shift 2)
subject: general
question: Which of the following methods is used to reduce earth resistance in an earthing system?

options.text: Reducing the distance between the earth and the neutral
Increasing the depth of the ground electrode

solution:
__**Explanation:**__

**Correct Option: Increasing the Depth of the Ground Electrode **

**Introduction:** In electrical systems, earthing plays a critical role in ensuring safety by providing a path for fault currents to safely dissipate into the earth. The effectiveness of an earthing system depends significantly on its earth resistance, which is the resistance offered by the grounding electrode and surrounding soil to the flow of electric current into the earth. A lower earth resistance is desirable for effective fault current dissipation, and several methods can be employed to achieve this. Among these, increasing the depth of the ground electrode is a widely recognized and effective method for reducing earth resistance.

**Why Increasing the Depth of the Ground Electrode Reduces Earth Resistance:**

 
• **Soil Resistivity Decreases with Depth:** The resistivity of soil tends to decrease as we go deeper underground. This is because deeper layers of soil are often more compact, have higher moisture content, and may contain dissolved salts, all of which contribute to better conductivity. By driving the ground electrode deeper, it comes into contact with these lower-resistivity layers, thereby reducing the overall earth resistance.
 
• **Improved Contact with the Earth:** A deeper electrode has a larger contact area with the earth. The increased surface area for current dissipation helps in lowering the resistance of the earthing system.
 
• **Bypassing High-Resistivity Layers:** In many locations, the top layers of soil may have higher resistivity due to dryness, loose texture, or contamination. By increasing the depth of the electrode, these problematic layers can be bypassed, allowing the electrode to reach more conductive soil layers.
 
• **Enhanced Fault Current Handling:** A deeper electrode can handle higher fault currents more effectively because of the reduced resistance. This ensures that the grounding system remains efficient even during high-current fault conditions.
